items.stem: Which tissue carries water from the roots to the leaves?
items.answer: Xylem
items.markingKey: Xylem vessels carry water and mineral ions upwards.

items.stem: Explain how root hair cells are adapted for taking in water.
items.answer: Each has a long, thin extension that gives a large surface area in close contact with soil water, so more water can enter.
items.markingKey: large surface area [1]; more water absorbed / contact with soil water [1] [2]

items.stem: A celery stalk is stood in water containing red dye. After a few hours, red dots are seen when the stalk is cut across. Explain this observation.
items.answer: The dyed water has travelled up the xylem vessels; the dots are the xylem vessels arranged in bundles.
items.markingKey: dye carried in xylem [1]; dots are xylem vessels / bundles [1] [2]

items.stem: Jonas stands two white rose stems in water containing blue dye, one in sunlight and one in a dark cupboard. After 45 minutes the dye has risen 36 mm in the first and 14 mm in the second. Calculate the rate of movement of the dye in each stem in mm per minute.
items.answer: 0.8 mm/min and 0.311 mm/min

items.stem: Yusuf stands two stems of busy lizzie plants in water containing blue dye, one in a warm, bright, breezy room and one in a cool, dark room. After 30 minutes the dye has risen 30 mm in the first and 12 mm in the second. (a) Calculate the rate of movement in each stem. (b) Name the tissue the dye moves through. (c) Explain the difference between the two results.
items.answer: (a) 1 and 0.4 mm/min (b) Xylem (c) Conditions in a warm, bright, breezy room increase evaporation of water from the leaves (transpiration), which pulls water up the xylem faster.
items.markingKey: (a) both rates [1] (b) xylem [1] (c) more evaporation / transpiration [1] [3]

items.stem: Ines investigates water movement in plants using celery stalks and coloured water. (a) Explain how water is moved up to the leaves. (b) Suggest why florists cut the bottom of stems under water before placing them in a vase.
items.answer: (a) Water evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out through stomata; this pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem. (b) Air bubbles can enter and block the xylem; cutting under water keeps the water column continuous so water can be taken up.
items.markingKey: (a) evaporation / transpiration from leaves [1]; pulls water up xylem [1] [2] (b) air blocks xylem [1]; cutting under water prevents this [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the structure of xylem helps it to transport water.
items.answer: It forms continuous hollow tubes with no end walls, so water can flow without obstruction; lignin keeps the tubes open and strong.
items.markingKey: continuous hollow tubes / no end walls [1]; lignin keeps them open [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a plant often wilts after it is moved from one pot to another.
items.answer: Root hairs are easily damaged during transplanting, so the plant absorbs less water and its cells lose firmness.
items.markingKey: root hairs damaged [1]; less water absorbed so wilting [1] [2]

items.stem: Kenji says: "Water enters a plant through its leaves." Explain why Kenji is wrong.
items.answer: Water is absorbed mainly through the root hair cells; leaves lose water through stomata.
items.markingKey: root hairs absorb water [1]; leaves lose water [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel stands two white carnation stems in water containing blue dye, one in sunlight and one in a dark cupboard. After 30 minutes the dye has risen 36 mm in the first and 22 mm in the second. Calculate the rate of movement of the dye in each stem in mm per minute.
items.answer: 1.2 mm/min and 0.733 mm/min

items.stem: Sofia stands two stems of busy lizzie plants in water containing blue dye, one in a warm, bright, breezy room and one in a cool, dark room. After 30 minutes the dye has risen 48 mm in the first and 19 mm in the second. (a) Calculate the rate of movement in each stem. (b) Name the tissue the dye moves through. (c) Explain the difference between the two results.
items.answer: (a) 1.6 and 0.633 mm/min (b) Xylem (c) Conditions in a warm, bright, breezy room increase evaporation of water from the leaves (transpiration), which pulls water up the xylem faster.
items.markingKey: (a) both rates [1] (b) xylem [1] (c) more evaporation / transpiration [1] [3]

items.stem: Jonas investigates water movement in plants using celery stalks and coloured water. (a) Explain how water is moved up to the leaves. (b) Suggest why florists cut the bottom of stems under water before placing them in a vase. (c) Give two reasons why leaves need a constant supply of water.
items.answer: (a) Water evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out through stomata; this pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem. (b) Air bubbles can enter and block the xylem; cutting under water keeps the water column continuous so water can be taken up. (c) Water is a reactant in photosynthesis; it keeps cells firm for support; it cools leaves as it evaporates.
items.markingKey: (a) evaporation / transpiration from leaves [1]; pulls water up xylem [1] [2] (b) air blocks xylem [1]; cutting under water prevents this [1] [2] (c) any two [1] each [2]

items.stem: What is transpiration?
options: The uptake of water by roots
The making of glucose in leaves
The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant
The transport of sugar in phloem
items.answer: The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant
items.markingKey: Water evaporates from leaf cells and diffuses out, mainly through stomata.

items.stem: Explain why transpiration is faster on a windy day.
items.answer: Wind blows away water vapour from around the leaf, keeping a steep concentration gradient so water vapour diffuses out faster.
items.markingKey: vapour removed [1]; steeper gradient / faster diffusion [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why transpiration is faster in bright light.
items.answer: Stomata open wider in light (for photosynthesis), so more water vapour can diffuse out.
items.markingKey: stomata open [1]; more water vapour lost [1] [2]

items.stem: Nadia sets up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The air bubble moves 20 mm in 4 minutes in still air and 60 mm in 4 minutes with a fan blowing. Calculate the rate of bubble movement in each condition in mm per minute.
items.answer: 5 and 15 mm/min

items.stem: Aisha sets up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The air bubble moves 8 mm in 2 minutes in the shade and 20 mm in 2 minutes in bright light. (a) Calculate both rates. (b) Explain why the rate is higher in bright light.
items.answer: (a) 4 and 10 mm/min (b) Stomata open wider, so more water vapour can diffuse out.
items.markingKey: (a) both rates [1] (b) correct factor [1]; explanation [1] [3]

items.stem: Priya coats four similar leaves with petroleum jelly (which blocks stomata) and hangs them up for 48 hours. Mass of each leaf at the start → end: A (no petroleum jelly): 2.4 g → 1.49 g; B (upper surface coated): 2.5 g → 1.85 g; C (lower surface coated): 2.2 g → 1.94 g; D (both surfaces coated): 2.2 g → 2.16 g. (a) Calculate the percentage loss in mass of leaf A. (b) Suggest why leaf D still lost a small amount of mass. (c) Name the process by which the leaves lose mass.
items.answer: (a) 37.9% (b) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating. (c) Transpiration (evaporation and diffusion of water vapour).
items.markingKey: (a) (2.4 − 1.49) ÷ 2.4 × 100 [1] = 37.9% [1] [2] (b) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating [1] (c) Transpiration (evaporation and diffusion of water vapour) [1]

items.stem: Which condition increases the rate of transpiration?
items.answer: Higher temperature
items.markingKey: Warmer air speeds up evaporation and diffusion of water vapour.

items.stem: Explain why the shoot for a potometer is cut under water.
items.answer: To stop air entering the xylem, which would block the flow of water and give false readings.
items.markingKey: prevents air bubbles in xylem [1]; flow not blocked [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why plants in hot, dry places often close their stomata in the middle of the day.
items.answer: To reduce water loss by transpiration and stop the plant wilting, although this also reduces carbon dioxide uptake.
items.markingKey: reduce water loss [1]; less CO₂ / photosynthesis as a cost [1] [2]

items.stem: In a test, Sofia writes: "Transpiration happens fastest on cold, still, humid nights." Identify the error and give the correct science.
items.answer: These conditions slow transpiration: it is fastest when warm, bright, windy and dry.
items.markingKey: conditions given slow it [1]; correct fast conditions [1] [2]

items.stem: Leila sets up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The air bubble moves 12 mm in 10 minutes in the shade and 30 mm in 10 minutes in bright light. Calculate the rate of bubble movement in each condition in mm per minute.
items.answer: 1.2 and 3 mm/min

items.stem: Kenji coats four similar leaves with petroleum jelly (which blocks stomata) and hangs them up for 48 hours. Mass of each leaf at the start → end: A (no petroleum jelly): 2.5 g → 1.55 g; B (upper surface coated): 2.5 g → 1.8 g; C (lower surface coated): 2.8 g → 2.46 g; D (both surfaces coated): 2.5 g → 2.42 g. (a) Suggest why leaf D still lost a small amount of mass. (b) Name the process by which the leaves lose mass. (c) Predict how the results would change if the leaves were hung in front of a fan, and explain why.
items.answer: (a) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating. (b) Transpiration (evaporation and diffusion of water vapour). (c) All uncoated surfaces would lose mass faster, because moving air removes water vapour and steepens the gradient.
items.markingKey: (a) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating [1] (b) Transpiration (evaporation and diffusion of water vapour) [1] (c) faster loss [1]; vapour removed [1] [2]

items.stem: Where in the body is urea made?
items.answer: In the liver
items.markingKey: The liver breaks down excess amino acids and makes urea.

items.stem: Explain why the blood in the renal vein contains less urea than the blood in the renal artery.
items.answer: The kidneys filter urea out of the blood into the urine, so blood leaving the kidney has less urea.
items.markingKey: kidneys filter / remove urea [1]; into urine [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a healthy person’s urine contains no glucose even though glucose is filtered from the blood.
items.answer: All the filtered glucose is reabsorbed back into the blood because the body needs it for respiration.
items.markingKey: glucose reabsorbed [1]; needed for respiration [1] [2]

items.stem: The kidneys filter 180 litres of fluid from the blood each day; 1.6 litres leave the body as urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed.

The kidneys of an adult filter about 100 cm³ of fluid from the blood every minute. (a) Calculate the volume filtered in one day, in litres. (b) The person produces 1.8 litres of urine a day. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed.

The kidneys of an adult filter about 110 cm³ of fluid from the blood every minute. (a) Calculate the volume filtered in one day, in litres. (b) The person produces 2 litres of urine a day. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed. (c) Explain why it is important that most of the filtered fluid is reabsorbed.
items.answer: (a) 110 × 60 × 24 = 158 400 cm³ = 158.4 litres (b) 98.7% (c) Otherwise the body would lose huge amounts of water (and glucose and salts) and quickly become dehydrated.
items.markingKey: (a) 110 × 1440 [1] = 158.4 litres [1] (b) (158.4 − 2) ÷ 158.4 × 100 = 98.7% [1] (c) prevents dehydration / keeps useful substances [1] [4]

items.stem: Data from a healthy volunteer, Isla: urea concentration in blood entering the kidney 0.28 g/dm³; blood leaving the kidney 0.02 g/dm³; urine 18 g/dm³. (a) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the blood entering the kidney. (b) Suggest what would happen to the urea concentration in the blood if both kidneys failed, and how this can be treated.
items.answer: (a) 64.3 times (b) It would rise to toxic levels; treatment by dialysis (a machine filters the blood) or a kidney transplant.
items.markingKey: (a) 18 ÷ 0.28 [1] = 64.3 [1] [2] (b) urea rises / toxic [1]; dialysis or transplant [1] [2]

items.stem: Data from a healthy volunteer, Mohammed: urea concentration in blood entering the kidney 0.28 g/dm³; blood leaving the kidney 0.02 g/dm³; urine 22 g/dm³. (a) Explain why the urea concentration is lower in the renal vein than in the renal artery. (b) Suggest what would happen to the urea concentration in the blood if both kidneys failed, and how this can be treated. (c) Name the tube that carries urine away from each kidney.
items.answer: (a) The kidney filters urea out of the blood and passes it into the urine. (b) It would rise to toxic levels; treatment by dialysis (a machine filters the blood) or a kidney transplant. (c) Ureter.
items.markingKey: (a) urea filtered out [1]; into urine [1] [2] (b) urea rises / toxic [1]; dialysis or transplant [1] [2] (c) Ureter [1]

items.stem: Urea is made from the breakdown of …
items.answer: excess amino acids
items.markingKey: Amino acids not needed are broken down; the nitrogen-containing part becomes urea.

items.stem: Explain why urine is darker and more concentrated on a hot day.
items.answer: More water is lost in sweat, so the kidneys reabsorb more water and produce a smaller volume of concentrated urine.
items.markingKey: water lost in sweat [1]; more water reabsorbed / less urine [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel says: "Faeces are an example of excretion." Explain why Daniel is wrong.
items.answer: Faeces are mostly undigested food that never entered cells, so their removal is egestion, not excretion.
items.markingKey: faeces = egestion [1]; excretion is waste of metabolism [1] [2]

items.stem: The kidneys of Nadia filter 144 litres of fluid from the blood each day and produce 1.8 litres of urine. What is the volume of water reabsorbed each day?
items.answer: 142 litres

items.stem: In one day Hana gains water from drinks (1500 cm³), food (700 cm³) and respiration (400 cm³), and loses water in sweat (900 cm³), breath (350 cm³), faeces (100 cm³) and urine. Calculate the volume of urine produced if the water gained equals the water lost.
items.answer: 1250 cm³

items.stem: The kidneys filter 172.8 litres of fluid from the blood each day; 2 litres leave the body as urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed.

In one day Nadia gains water from drinks (1500 cm³), food (900 cm³) and respiration (350 cm³), and loses water in sweat (900 cm³), breath (350 cm³), faeces (100 cm³) and urine. (a) Calculate the volume of urine needed to balance the water gained and lost. (b) Name the organs that control the volume of urine.
items.answer: (a) 1400 cm³ (b) The kidneys.
items.markingKey: (a) total gain 2750 [1]; urine 1400 cm³ [1] (b) kidneys [1] [3]

items.stem: Data from a healthy volunteer, Yusuf: urea concentration in blood entering the kidney 0.35 g/dm³; blood leaving the kidney 0.04 g/dm³; urine 18 g/dm³. (a) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the blood entering the kidney. (b) Explain why urea is much more concentrated in urine than in blood.
items.answer: (a) 51.4 times (b) Most of the water filtered is reabsorbed into the blood, but urea is not, so it becomes concentrated.
items.markingKey: (a) 18 ÷ 0.35 [1] = 51.4 [1] [2] (b) water reabsorbed [1]; urea left behind [1] [2]

items.stem: Data from a healthy volunteer, Kwame: urea concentration in blood entering the kidney 0.3 g/dm³; blood leaving the kidney 0.03 g/dm³; urine 20 g/dm³. (a) Explain why urea is much more concentrated in urine than in blood. (b) Suggest what would happen to the urea concentration in the blood if both kidneys failed, and how this can be treated. (c) Name the tube that carries urine away from each kidney.
items.answer: (a) Most of the water filtered is reabsorbed into the blood, but urea is not, so it becomes concentrated. (b) It would rise to toxic levels; treatment by dialysis (a machine filters the blood) or a kidney transplant. (c) Ureter.
items.markingKey: (a) water reabsorbed [1]; urea left behind [1] [2] (b) urea rises / toxic [1]; dialysis or transplant [1] [2] (c) Ureter [1]

items.stem: What is the main function of the placenta?
options: Exchange of substances between the mother’s blood and the fetus’s blood
items.answer: Exchange of substances between the mother’s blood and the fetus’s blood
items.markingKey: Oxygen and nutrients pass to the fetus; carbon dioxide and urea pass to the mother.

items.stem: Which substance passes from the fetus to the mother across the placenta?
items.answer: Carbon dioxide
items.markingKey: Waste such as CO₂ and urea pass to the mother’s blood.

items.stem: Explain why babies of mothers who smoke during pregnancy tend to have a lower birth mass.
items.answer: Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen carried in the mother’s blood and nicotine narrows blood vessels, so the fetus gets less oxygen and nutrients and grows less.
items.markingKey: less oxygen (CO) [1]; less nutrient supply / narrowed vessels [1]; slower growth [1] [3]

items.stem: A hospital in Hanoi records the mean birth mass of babies grouped by how much their mothers smoked during pregnancy: non-smokers: 3.55 kg; 1–9 cigarettes a day: 3.37 kg; 10–19 cigarettes a day: 3.25 kg; 20 or more cigarettes a day: 3.1 kg. Calculate the difference in mean birth mass between babies of non-smokers and of mothers smoking 20 or more a day.

A health clinic in Karachi is preparing a leaflet for pregnant women about keeping the fetus healthy. (a) Explain how waste substances made by the fetus are removed. (b) Suggest why advice on alcohol is “none at all” rather than “drink a little”.
items.answer: (a) Carbon dioxide and urea diffuse from the fetus’s blood into the mother’s blood in the placenta; the mother excretes them. (b) No safe level is known; even small amounts reach the developing brain, so the safest advice is to avoid it completely.
items.markingKey: (a) diffuse into mother’s blood [1]; excreted by mother’s lungs / kidneys [1] [2] (b) no known safe level [1]; small amounts can harm developing organs [1] [2]

items.stem: Which structure connects the fetus to the placenta?
items.answer: The umbilical cord
items.markingKey: The cord carries the fetus’s blood to and from the placenta.

items.stem: A hospital in Accra records the mean birth mass of babies grouped by how much their mothers smoked during pregnancy: non-smokers: 3.45 kg; 1–9 cigarettes a day: 3.25 kg; 10–19 cigarettes a day: 3.15 kg; 20 or more cigarettes a day: 3 kg. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in mean birth mass for mothers smoking 20 or more a day compared with non-smokers. (b) Explain how smoking causes this effect.
items.answer: (a) 13% (b) Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen the blood carries and nicotine narrows blood vessels, so the fetus gets less oxygen and nutrients across the placenta.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.45 ÷ 3.45 × 100 [1] = 13% [1] (b) less oxygen / nutrients reach fetus [1] [3]

items.stem: A hospital in Toronto records the mean birth mass of babies grouped by how much their mothers smoked during pregnancy: non-smokers: 3.4 kg; 1–9 cigarettes a day: 3.2 kg; 10–19 cigarettes a day: 3.12 kg; 20 or more cigarettes a day: 3 kg. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in mean birth mass for mothers smoking 20 or more a day compared with non-smokers. (b) Explain how smoking causes this effect. (c) Suggest why these data alone do not prove that smoking causes lower birth mass.
items.answer: (a) 11.8% (b) Carbon monoxide reduces the oxygen the blood carries and nicotine narrows blood vessels, so the fetus gets less oxygen and nutrients across the placenta. (c) Other factors (diet, age, income, alcohol) may differ between the groups; a correlation does not prove cause.
items.markingKey: (a) 0.4 ÷ 3.4 × 100 [1] = 11.8% [1] (b) less oxygen / nutrients reach fetus [1]; CO or nicotine named [1] (c) other variables / correlation [1] [5]

items.stem: A health clinic in Dhaka is preparing a leaflet for pregnant women about keeping the fetus healthy. (a) Explain why the leaflet should advise eating foods rich in protein and iron. (b) Suggest why advice on alcohol is “none at all” rather than “drink a little”.
items.answer: (a) Protein is needed to build new cells for growth; iron is needed to make haemoglobin for the fetus’s red blood cells. (b) No safe level is known; even small amounts reach the developing brain, so the safest advice is to avoid it completely.
items.markingKey: (a) protein for growth [1]; iron for haemoglobin [1] [2] (b) no known safe level [1]; small amounts can harm developing organs [1] [2]

items.stem: Which cells take in most of the water entering a plant?
items.answer: Root hair cells
items.markingKey: Root hairs give a large surface area in contact with soil water.

items.stem: Explain what “pulls” water up the xylem of a tall tree.
items.answer: Water evaporates from the leaves and leaves through stomata; this pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem from the roots.
items.markingKey: evaporation / loss from leaves [1]; pulls water column up [1] [2]

items.stem: Zara stands two white carnation stems in water containing blue dye, one next to a fan and one in still air. After 45 minutes the dye has risen 42 mm in the first and 21 mm in the second. Calculate the rate of movement of the dye in each stem in mm per minute.
items.answer: 0.933 mm/min and 0.467 mm/min

items.stem: Samuel stands two white carnation stems in water containing blue dye, one in sunlight and one in a dark cupboard. After 40 minutes the dye has risen 60 mm in the first and 36 mm in the second. (a) Calculate the rate of movement in each stem. (b) Name the tissue the dye moves through. (c) Explain the difference between the two results.
items.answer: (a) 1.5 and 0.9 mm/min (b) Xylem (c) Conditions in sunlight increase evaporation of water from the leaves (transpiration), which pulls water up the xylem faster.
items.markingKey: (a) both rates [1] (b) xylem [1] (c) more evaporation / transpiration [1] [3]

items.stem: A gardener in Madrid notices that a 30 m tall tree must move large volumes of water from its roots to its highest leaves every day. (a) Name the tissue that carries water up the stem and describe two features that suit it to this job. (b) Suggest why florists cut the bottom of stems under water before placing them in a vase.
items.answer: (a) Xylem: long hollow tubes with no end walls; walls strengthened with lignin. (b) Air bubbles can enter and block the xylem; cutting under water keeps the water column continuous so water can be taken up.
items.markingKey: (a) xylem [1]; two features [1] [2] (b) air blocks xylem [1]; cutting under water prevents this [1] [2]

items.stem: Which cells open and close the stomata?
items.answer: Guard cells
items.markingKey: A pair of guard cells surrounds each stoma.

items.stem: Explain why a potometer measures water uptake rather than exactly the rate of transpiration.
items.answer: Some of the water taken up is used by the plant (e.g. in photosynthesis or to keep cells firm) and is not lost.
items.markingKey: some water used by plant [1]; uptake ≠ loss exactly [1] [2]

items.stem: Arjun sets up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The air bubble moves 10 mm in 5 minutes inside a plastic bag (humid) and 20 mm in 5 minutes in open, dry air. Calculate the rate of bubble movement in each condition in mm per minute.
items.answer: 2 and 4 mm/min

items.stem: Tomás coats four similar leaves with petroleum jelly (which blocks stomata) and hangs them up for 36 hours. Mass of each leaf at the start → end: A (no petroleum jelly): 2 g → 1.32 g; B (upper surface coated): 2 g → 1.52 g; C (lower surface coated): 2 g → 1.76 g; D (both surfaces coated): 2.8 g → 2.72 g. (a) Calculate the percentage loss in mass of leaf B. (b) Suggest why leaf D still lost a small amount of mass.
items.answer: (a) 24% (b) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating.
items.markingKey: (a) (2 − 1.52) ÷ 2 × 100 [1] = 24% [1] [2] (b) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating [1]

items.stem: Mei coats four similar leaves with petroleum jelly (which blocks stomata) and hangs them up for 48 hours. Mass of each leaf at the start → end: A (no petroleum jelly): 2 g → 1.32 g; B (upper surface coated): 2.5 g → 1.85 g; C (lower surface coated): 2.8 g → 2.58 g; D (both surfaces coated): 2.5 g → 2.42 g. (a) Explain why percentage loss is used instead of the loss in grams. (b) Explain why leaf C lost much less mass than leaf B. (c) Suggest why leaf D still lost a small amount of mass.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which blood vessel carries blood into a kidney? (b) Which tube carries urine from a kidney to the bladder?
items.answer: (a) Renal artery (b) Ureter
items.markingKey: (a) Renal artery in; renal vein out. (b) Each kidney has a ureter leading to the bladder.

items.stem: Describe the difference between excretion and egestion.
items.answer: Excretion removes waste made by cells (urea, CO₂); egestion removes undigested food (faeces) that was never inside cells.
items.markingKey: excretion = metabolic waste [1]; egestion = undigested food [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why kidney failure is life-threatening if untreated.
items.answer: Urea, excess water and salts build up in the blood; urea is toxic and water/salt balance is lost.
items.markingKey: urea builds up / toxic [1]; water and salt balance lost [1] [2]

items.answer: 600 cm³

items.stem: Explain why a pregnant woman is advised not to drink alcohol.
items.answer: Alcohol crosses the placenta into the fetus’s blood and can damage the developing brain and organs.
items.markingKey: crosses placenta [1]; damages development [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel says: "The placenta stops all harmful substances reaching the baby." Explain why Samuel is wrong.
items.answer: Many harmful substances such as alcohol, nicotine, some drugs and some viruses can cross the placenta.

items.stem: A hospital in Dubai records the mean birth mass of babies grouped by how much their mothers smoked during pregnancy: non-smokers: 3.55 kg; 1–9 cigarettes a day: 3.37 kg; 10–19 cigarettes a day: 3.27 kg; 20 or more cigarettes a day: 3.17 kg. Calculate the difference in mean birth mass between babies of non-smokers and of mothers smoking 20 or more a day.
Which statement describes xylem vessels?
options: Tubes that carry sugars down to the roots
Long, hollow tubes made of dead cells with no end walls
items.answer: Long, hollow tubes made of dead cells with no end walls
items.markingKey: Xylem cells are dead, lose their end walls and form continuous tubes strengthened by lignin.

items.stem: Suggest why xylem tissue is found in the veins of leaves.
items.answer: To deliver water and mineral ions to all the leaf cells for photosynthesis and to keep them firm.
items.markingKey: delivers water to leaf cells [1]; for photosynthesis / support [1] [2]

items.stem: Daniel stands two white carnation stems in water containing blue dye, one next to a fan and one in still air. After 45 minutes the dye has risen 36 mm in the first and 22 mm in the second. Calculate the rate of movement of the dye in each stem in mm per minute.
items.answer: 0.8 mm/min and 0.489 mm/min

items.stem: Zara stands two white rose stems in water containing blue dye, one next to a fan and one in still air. After 45 minutes the dye has risen 36 mm in the first and 14 mm in the second. (a) Calculate the rate of movement in each stem. (b) Name the tissue the dye moves through. (c) Explain the difference between the two results.
items.answer: (a) 0.8 and 0.311 mm/min (b) Xylem (c) Conditions next to a fan increase evaporation of water from the leaves (transpiration), which pulls water up the xylem faster.
items.markingKey: (a) both rates [1] (b) xylem [1] (c) more evaporation / transpiration [1] [3]

items.stem: A gardener in Mexico City notices that a 80 m tall tree must move large volumes of water from its roots to its highest leaves every day. (a) Name the tissue that carries water up the stem and describe two features that suit it to this job. (b) Suggest why florists cut the bottom of stems under water before placing them in a vase.
items.answer: (a) Xylem: long hollow tubes with no end walls; walls strengthened with lignin. (b) Air bubbles can enter and block the xylem; cutting under water keeps the water column continuous so water can be taken up.
items.markingKey: (a) xylem [1]; two features [1] [2] (b) air blocks xylem [1]; cutting under water prevents this [1] [2]

items.stem: On which surface of most leaves are most stomata found?
items.answer: The lower surface
items.markingKey: More stomata underneath reduces water loss from direct sunlight.

items.stem: Explain why transpiration is useful to a plant.
items.answer: It pulls water and mineral ions up the xylem to the leaves, and evaporation cools the leaves.
items.markingKey: transport of water and minerals [1]; cooling [1] [2]

items.stem: Sipho sets up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The air bubble moves 8 mm in 10 minutes inside a plastic bag (humid) and 16 mm in 10 minutes in open, dry air. Calculate the rate of bubble movement in each condition in mm per minute.
items.answer: 0.8 and 1.6 mm/min

items.stem: Isla sets up a potometer with a leafy shoot. The air bubble moves 18 mm in 4 minutes inside a plastic bag (humid) and 45 mm in 4 minutes in open, dry air. (a) Calculate both rates. (b) Explain why the rate is higher in open, dry air.
items.answer: (a) 4.5 and 11.3 mm/min (b) Dry air has less water vapour, so the concentration gradient is steeper and diffusion is faster.
items.markingKey: (a) both rates [1] (b) correct factor [1]; explanation [1] [3]

items.stem: Chloe coats four similar leaves with petroleum jelly (which blocks stomata) and hangs them up for 24 hours. Mass of each leaf at the start → end: A (no petroleum jelly): 2.8 g → 1.96 g; B (upper surface coated): 2.5 g → 1.85 g; C (lower surface coated): 2.2 g → 1.98 g; D (both surfaces coated): 2 g → 1.94 g. (a) Calculate the percentage loss in mass of leaf C. (b) Explain why leaf C lost much less mass than leaf B. (c) Suggest why leaf D still lost a small amount of mass.
items.answer: (a) 10% (b) Most stomata are on the lower surface; coating it blocks most of the routes for water vapour to leave. (c) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating.
items.markingKey: (a) (2.2 − 1.98) ÷ 2.2 × 100 [1] = 10% [1] [2] (b) most stomata on lower surface [1]; blocked so less water lost [1] [2] (c) Some water evaporates through the waxy cuticle or through gaps in the coating [1]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Which blood vessel carries blood into a kidney? (b) Which organ excretes carbon dioxide?
items.answer: (a) Renal artery (b) The lungs
items.markingKey: (a) Renal artery in; renal vein out. (b) CO₂ from respiration is excreted by the lungs.

items.stem: Describe the path of urine from where it is made to where it leaves the body.
items.answer: Kidney → ureter → bladder (stored) → urethra → out of the body.
items.markingKey: kidney to bladder via ureter [1]; bladder to outside via urethra [1] [2]

items.stem: Yusuf says: "The kidneys make urea." Explain why Yusuf is wrong.
items.answer: Urea is made in the liver; the kidneys remove it from the blood into the urine.
items.markingKey: liver makes urea [1]; kidneys remove it [1] [2]

items.stem: The kidneys filter 180 litres of fluid from the blood each day; 1.5 litres leave the body as urine. Calculate the percentage of the filtered fluid that is reabsorbed.

In one day Grace gains water from drinks (1200 cm³), food (900 cm³) and respiration (400 cm³), and loses water in sweat (1200 cm³), breath (300 cm³), faeces (100 cm³) and urine. Calculate the volume of urine produced if the water gained equals the water lost.
items.answer: 900 cm³

items.stem: Data from a healthy volunteer, Zara: urea concentration in blood entering the kidney 0.3 g/dm³; blood leaving the kidney 0.03 g/dm³; urine 20 g/dm³. (a) Explain why the urea concentration is lower in the renal vein than in the renal artery. (b) State where urea is made and from what.
items.answer: (a) The kidney filters urea out of the blood and passes it into the urine. (b) In the liver, from the breakdown of excess amino acids.
items.markingKey: (a) urea filtered out [1]; into urine [1] [2] (b) liver [1]; excess amino acids [1] [2]

items.stem: Data from a healthy volunteer, Yusuf: urea concentration in blood entering the kidney 0.4 g/dm³; blood leaving the kidney 0.05 g/dm³; urine 18 g/dm³. (a) Calculate how many times more concentrated urea is in the urine than in the blood entering the kidney. (b) Explain why the urea concentration is lower in the renal vein than in the renal artery. (c) Explain why urea is much more concentrated in urine than in blood.
items.answer: (a) 45 times (b) The kidney filters urea out of the blood and passes it into the urine. (c) Most of the water filtered is reabsorbed into the blood, but urea is not, so it becomes concentrated.
items.markingKey: (a) 18 ÷ 0.4 [1] = 45 [1] [2] (b) urea filtered out [1]; into urine [1] [2] (c) water reabsorbed [1]; urea left behind [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how the placenta is adapted for exchange of substances.
items.answer: It has a very large surface area (many villi), thin walls between the two blood supplies and a good blood supply, so diffusion is fast.
items.markingKey: large surface area [1]; thin barrier / good blood supply [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel says: "A pregnant woman should eat for two, so she needs double the food." Explain why Samuel is wrong.
items.answer: She needs only a little more energy, but more of certain nutrients (protein, iron, calcium, folic acid); a balanced diet matters more than quantity.
items.markingKey: only slightly more energy [1]; specific nutrients / balance [1] [2]

items.stem: A hospital in Singapore records the mean birth mass of babies grouped by how much their mothers smoked during pregnancy: non-smokers: 3.5 kg; 1–9 cigarettes a day: 3.35 kg; 10–19 cigarettes a day: 3.18 kg; 20 or more cigarettes a day: 3.1 kg. Calculate the difference in mean birth mass between babies of non-smokers and of mothers smoking 20 or more a day.
items.answer: 0.4 kg
